prompt.context: A fast food chain was experiencing rapid growth. They had acquired several new locations and reapplied their business model in those new stores. They were disappointed that some of the stores seemed to do well, while others were barely breaking even.
prompt.question: How would you go about investigating this problem?

clarifying_info.q: Where were the older stores located?
clarifying_info.a: The firm's older stores were in predominantly lower income neighborhoods.

clarifying_info.q: Are the underperforming stores selling less product overall?
clarifying_info.a: The underperforming stores were actually selling more product per customer, but were attracting far fewer customers.

framework: Understand the specific nature of the problem at poor-performing stores: are revenues lower or costs higher?
Revenue drivers: number of customers and sales per customer (volume and mix)
Cost drivers: labor, real estate and facilities, food inputs and other variable costs
Investigate why new stores are attracting fewer customers across four dimensions: Price, Customers, Location, Product, and Competition

questions.prompt: Are the underperforming stores generating lower revenue or higher costs compared to the well-performing stores?
questions.guidance: Candidate should disaggregate profitability into revenue (fewer customers vs. lower ticket size) and costs (labor, rent, food inputs). The clarifying info reveals the problem is on the customer-count side of revenue, not ticket size or costs.

questions.prompt: Why are the new stores attracting far fewer customers?
questions.guidance: Strong answers explore: Price (are prices misaligned with the new market?), Customer segmentation (who shops in the new locations vs. the old ones?), Location (mall vs. freestanding, neighborhood income level), Product (same menu everywhere?), and Competition (same or more competitors in new locations?). The key insight is that the new stores are in upscale malls where the brand is perceived as a low-price chain, which hurts customer traffic among the higher-income demographic.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors could explain why the new stores in upscale mall locations are underperforming?

categories.name: Price
ideas: Prices may be too high relative to brand perception
Prices may be too low relative to mall customer expectations — signaling low quality
Price positioning inconsistent with the surrounding retail environment

categories.name: Customer Segmentation
ideas: Mall shoppers skew higher income than the firm's traditional lower-income customer base
Different segments have different needs: convenience, quality, status signals
Low-income customers in old locations had fewer alternatives; mall customers have many options

categories.name: Location
ideas: Upscale malls attract a different demographic than standalone stores in lower-income neighborhoods
Mall food courts have higher competition density
Drive-thru convenience absent in mall food courts

categories.name: Product
ideas: Menu may not appeal to higher-income consumers who expect fresher or higher-quality options
Same menu reapplied without adapting to local tastes or segment preferences

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Old stores faced few competitors in lower-income areas
New mall stores face more fast-casual and upscale quick-service competitors
Brand image disadvantage vs. competitors in the upscale segment

categories.name: Brand Image
ideas: Firm is perceived as a low-price brand, which deters higher-income consumers
No brand repositioning done before entering new locations

recommendation: The core problem is a location-segment mismatch: the firm's brand and business model were optimized for lower-income neighborhoods with limited competition, but the new stores are in upscale malls serving a higher-income customer base who do not identify with the brand

The firm should either reposition its offering in the new locations (upgrade menu, redesign stores, adjust marketing) or exit high-end mall locations and expand instead in additional lower-income or suburban markets where the brand resonates
risks: Repositioning risks diluting the brand appeal in legacy low-income stores
Exiting mall locations may result in lease penalties or sunk real estate costs
Failing to act means the new stores will continue to drag on overall profitability
next_steps: Conduct customer research in both old and new store locations to confirm segmentation hypothesis
Pilot a menu or store-format upgrade in one or two mall locations to test repositioning
Evaluate lease exit options and associated costs for the worst-performing mall stores
Define a clear target customer profile before pursuing further expansion
